title: Image and likeness
hookLine: Orthodox teachers say we have God's image and grow into his likeness

lines: LET US MAKE MAN IN OUR IMAGE.
cards: "And God said, Let us make man in our image, after our likeness." That's Genesis, on the sixth day. Read it fast and it sounds like one idea said twice.
Some readers take it that way. But some early Christian teachers slowed right down on that pair. Two words, they said, two gifts: one you're born with, one you grow into.
That reading lives on in the Orthodox churches of the East, and it changes how a whole life looks. Today: image and likeness.

teach.h: THE IMAGE: GIVEN TO EVERY HUMAN.
teach.b: Day three hundred thirty-four met the image of God in Genesis. In this reading, the image is given, whole, to every human being.
The very next verse says it plainly: "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them." Nobody earns it. Nobody loses it.
A baby has it. A prisoner has it. The person who annoys you most has it.
Orthodox teachers speak of it as something like the stamp of the maker, and point to the mind and freedom that make a person a person.

The likeness is not a stamp but a resemblance. It's the image starting to show in how someone actually lives: patience, mercy and love growing in them slowly, like a child growing to look like a parent.
In Orthodox teaching, that growing is the whole Christian life, and it goes all the way: they call it theosis, becoming by grace like God.
Paul has a line that sounds like this kind of growth: "we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory." Not in one leap.
Other Christians read image and likeness as one idea said twice, and speak of growth with other words: sanctification, becoming holy. The shape is close.
But the two-word reading leaves a memorable picture: a gift that's already yours, and a face you grow into.

how: Orthodox Christians speak of growing from the image into the likeness of God, a lifelong path they call theosis, walked through prayer, the sacraments and love of neighbor; other churches speak of the same growth as sanctification.

o: God's outward look, copied in every human body
the image given to all; the likeness grown into
two names for the one face Adam was born with

games.q: image and likeness — tap the pairs.

s: in this reading, someone who does wrong loses the image of God
the image is given whole to every person. nobody earns it, and nobody loses it.
Genesis uses both words, image and likeness, in the same verse
"Let us make man in our image, after our likeness."
all Christians split image and likeness into two gifts
Orthodox teachers do; other Christians read the two words as one idea said twice.

games.q: you read Genesis: let us make man in our image, after our likeness. two words. what do Orthodox teachers do with them?
o: treat them as one idea said twice.
say the image is given, and the likeness is grown into.
say only some people get the image.
games.why: Orthodox teachers read two gifts: the image, given whole to everyone, and the likeness, grown into over a lifetime, from glory to glory.

practice: Hold in mind one person you find hard to be around, and remember that in this teaching they carry the image too, whole.
Then choose one quality you'd like to see grow in you, patience, gentleness, honesty or courage, and picture one small moment later today when it could show.
If you pray, ask for help to grow toward it; if not, just hold that moment clearly.

wordCard.voice: Image and likeness. In Orthodox teaching, the image of God is given to every person; the likeness is grown into, slowly, by grace.

orig.note: Hebrew: image. The first of the two words in Genesis 1:26; the second, likeness, is demut.

carryVoice: Your line: image given, likeness grown. It's slow work, done by grace. Back tomorrow, same hill.
